title: Xu, Five Punishments and Beyond — the penal codes of imperial China

1.title: Law as an instrument of cosmic balance
1.text: Chinese law and justice are AS OLD AS CHINESE HISTORY. One of the features that define an ancient civilisation is the EMERGENCE OF THE STATE (or of a ruler), and law and justice belong to the basic functions of a state. The starting point: THE RULING ELITES UNDERSTOOD LAW AS AN INSTRUMENT FOR MAINTAINING THE BALANCE BETWEEN THE TWO PRIMORDIAL FORCES OF THE COSMOS — YIN (negative, female, the moon, waters) AND YANG (positive, male, the sun, mountains) — WHICH MANIFESTS ITSELF IN HUMAN SOCIETY AS THE EXISTING POLITICAL-SOCIAL-MORAL ORDER. Chinese penal codes appeared in the pre-imperial period as prototypes and grew in the imperial era towards ever greater sophistication and comprehensiveness — their development was an INTEGRAL PART OF THE CONTINUOUS DEVELOPMENT OF THE CHINESE IMPERIAL SYSTEM, despite the regular succession of dynasties.

terms.def: The two primordial forces of the cosmos; their balance manifests itself in human society as the political-social-moral order which law is meant to maintain.

cards.q: How did the ruling elites in China understand the purpose of law?
cards.a: As an INSTRUMENT FOR MAINTAINING THE BALANCE BETWEEN YIN AND YANG, the two primordial forces of the cosmos, which manifests itself in human society as the existing POLITICAL-SOCIAL-MORAL ORDER. Law therefore maintains not merely order among people but the order of the universe.

2.title: From the inner self to the empire: the chain everything rests on
2.text: An influential Confucian creed from the ZHOU period (11th–3rd century BC): 'ONLY WHEN MINDS ARE RECTIFIED (ZHENGXIN) ARE PERSONS CULTIVATED (XIUSHEN); ONLY WHEN PERSONS ARE CULTIVATED ARE FAMILIES REGULATED (QIJIA); ONLY WHEN FAMILIES ARE REGULATED IS GOOD GOVERNANCE ACHIEVED (ZHIGUO); ONLY WHEN GOOD GOVERNANCE IS ACHIEVED IS THERE PEACE ALL UNDER HEAVEN (PINGTIANXIA).' That chain SELF → FAMILY → GOVERNANCE → ALL UNDER HEAVEN ties together the moral foundations of Chinese society which law was meant to support: its family system, its social structure, its morality and its governance. The whole order rested on the idea of INTERACTION AND HARMONY BETWEEN HEAVEN AND HUMAN SOCIETY, both underpinned by the balance of yin and yang — the historian BENJAMIN SCHWARTZ called this 'CORRELATIVE COSMOLOGY'.

cards.q: Recite the Confucian chain from the inner self to the world, and say what follows from it for law.
cards.a: Only when MINDS are rectified are PERSONS cultivated; only then are FAMILIES regulated; only then is GOOD GOVERNANCE achieved; and only then is there PEACE ALL UNDER HEAVEN. Law is meant to support this chain — which is why the penal codes protect the family system and the position of the emperor as one and the same thing.

3.title: The Mandate of Heaven and the boat on the water
3.text: The Shang and Zhou dynasties were founded by SHANG TANG and KING WU, each after a rebellion against the sitting ruler. To justify his rebellion KING WU CLAIMED THE MANDATE OF HEAVEN (TIANMING) and condemned the previous ruler for having FAILED THE WILL OF HEAVEN AND THE WISHES OF THE PEOPLE, thereby losing the mandate. Two of the most influential ideas grew out of these early notions: HEAVEN IS THE SUPREME COSMIC FORCE and THE RULER IS THE SON OF HEAVEN (TIANZI); and the PATRIARCHAL FAMILY SYSTEM, instituted by Heaven and held by the balance of yin and yang, is the foundation of the whole order. The two joined conveniently in the person of the ruler AS BOTH SON OF HEAVEN AND PARENT OF THE PEOPLE. MENCIUS put it most forcefully: the ruler's role is to FULFIL THE WILL OF HEAVEN AND CARE FOR THE PEOPLE AS A PARENT, with benevolent government. And XUN ZI added the metaphor that became a classic: the king of the state of Lu asked Confucius what dangers he faced, and Confucius answered: 'THE RULER IS THE BOAT AND THE COMMON PEOPLE ARE THE WATER; THE WATER CAN CARRY THE BOAT AND THE WATER CAN OVERTURN THE BOAT.' From this came the lasting notion that THE PEOPLE ARE THE FOUNDATION OF THE STATE (MINBEN). And the political consequence, repeated for two thousand years: THE IDEA THAT THE MANDATE OF HEAVEN CAN BE LOST BY FAILING TO DELIVER BENEVOLENT GOVERNMENT AND PASSED TO ANOTHER SON OF HEAVEN WAS INVOKED REPEATEDLY AND ROUTINELY BY THE FOUNDERS OF NEW DYNASTIES TO JUSTIFY OVERTHROWING THE PREVIOUS ONES.

terms.def: The Mandate of Heaven: the ruler's legitimacy, which can be lost by failing to deliver benevolent government — and which is therefore claimed by every successful rebel.
'The people are the foundation of the state' — from the metaphor of the boat and the water, which carries the boat and can also overturn it.

cards.q: What is the Mandate of Heaven and what political function did it serve?
cards.a: The legitimacy of the ruler as SON OF HEAVEN, which can be LOST by failing to deliver benevolent government and which then passes to another. Its function was twofold: whoever overthrew a dynasty justified the overthrow by it (King Wu against the Shang), and at the same time every ruler was pressed by it to govern benevolently.

cards.q: Quote the metaphor of the boat and the water and say what came out of it.
cards.a: 'The ruler is the boat and the common people are the water; the water can carry the boat and the water can overturn the boat' — attributed to Confucius in Xun Zi's account. From it came the lasting notion of MINBEN, that THE PEOPLE ARE THE FOUNDATION OF THE STATE, which Confucian scholars cited for centuries as a moral-political admonition to the ruler.

4.title: Was it believed, or was it rhetoric?
4.text: Xu puts the question directly, and it is worth being able to answer: WAS THE IDEA OF HEAVEN-HUMAN INTERACTION A GENUINE BELIEF, OR MERELY POLITICAL RHETORIC — of officials, to press the emperor towards benevolence, and of the emperor, to press officials into performing their duties properly? THE ANSWER: PROBABLY BOTH. The evidence: Emperor TAIZONG of the Tang issued at least six amnesties, the first on his accession and all the others IN RESPONSE TO NATURAL DISASTERS (storms and floods, drought, locusts). In 737 the court reported to Emperor XUANZONG that only 58 capital offenders had been executed in the whole realm AND THAT MAGPIES HAD BUILT NESTS IN THE TREES OF THE COURT GARDEN, where birds had previously not come because of the excessive 'MURDEROUS ATMOSPHERE' (SHAQI) OF YIN — and the emperor ordered a banquet and rewards. The Song official BAO ZHENG, faced with winter thunder, eclipses, comets and earthquakes, advised the emperor to lower taxes, listen to honest opinions and reward virtue 'IN RESPONSE TO THE WARNINGS FROM HEAVEN'. And Emperor KANGXI in 1697 on a predicted eclipse: 'SOLAR ECLIPSES CAN BE CALCULATED, YET KINGS AND EMPERORS HAVE ALWAYS BEEN ALARMED AND, TAKING WARNING, HAVE SOUGHT TO IMPROVE HUMAN AFFAIRS… I THINK THESE EVENTS ARISE FROM AN EXCESS OF YIN. HOW CAN ANYONE SAY THEY HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH HUMAN AFFAIRS?' — AND BY 'EXCESS OF YIN' HE MEANT THAT TOO MANY PEOPLE HAD BEEN EXECUTED OR WRONGLY PUNISHED. In 1675, during a drought, he accordingly ordered a review of all criminal cases and the correction of wrongful convictions. And the counter-evidence: WU NA, in his commentary on model cases, implied THAT IN HIS VIEW DROUGHTS AND STORMS HAD NO DIRECT CONNECTION WITH THE ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE, and clever officials solved murders by manipulating popular belief in local earth gods — which suggests THEY DID NOT BELIEVE IN THOSE GODS THEMSELVES. They nevertheless shared the basic idea of JUSTICE AS THE ACCORD OF HEAVENLY REASON, STATE LAW AND HUMAN RELATIONS, AND AS THE BALANCE OF YIN AND YANG.

cards.q: Was the idea of Heaven-human interaction a belief or rhetoric?
cards.a: Probably BOTH. Emperors issued amnesties after natural disasters, and Kangxi read floods and eclipses as an 'excess of yin', that is, as a sign that too many people had been executed or unjustly punished. At the same time Wu Na commented that droughts and storms have no direct connection with the administration of justice, and officials manipulated popular belief in earth gods they did not themselves believe in.

cards.q: What did 'an excess of yin' mean in Emperor Kangxi's mouth, and what followed from it in practice?
cards.a: That TOO MANY PEOPLE had been executed or wrongly punished. In practice a review followed: in 1675, during a drought, he ordered senior officials to go through all criminal cases and correct wrongful convictions; in 1695, after an earthquake, he proclaimed a general amnesty.

5.title: Confucianism and Legalism: the quarrel about human nature
5.text: Both schools agreed that the ruler and the elites should CARE (YANG) for the common people as parents care for children — which includes protection, nourishment, education, discipline and punishment. THEY DIFFERED ON HOW. The CONFUCIANS believed that PEOPLE ARE BORN GOOD, even if 'petty persons' tend to go astray; order should therefore be maintained by MORAL FORCES such as rites and propriety, instilled through education. Confucius: REGULATING THE PEOPLE BY ORDERS AND PUNISHMENTS WILL DETER THEM FROM WRONGDOING BUT WILL NOT TEACH THEM WHAT TO BE ASHAMED OF; LEADING THE PEOPLE BY VIRTUE AND PROPRIETY WILL TEACH THEM NOT TO DO WHAT IS SHAMEFUL. HAN FEI, the Legalist, shared with the Confucians the idea of a hierarchical order sanctioned by Heaven — 'the minister serves the ruler, the son the father, the wife the husband; when these three are in order, there is peace all under heaven'. BUT the Legalists believed that HUMAN NATURE IS INHERENTLY BAD BECAUSE PEOPLE HAVE BODILY DESIRES, and they stressed THE ROLE OF LAW AND PUNISHMENT. Their idea was that THE DETERRENT EFFECT WOULD BE SUCH THAT IN THE END THERE WOULD BE NO NEED TO PUNISH AT ALL, because everyone would learn to obey the law having seen examples of punishment. In other words: THE LEGALISTS CARED ABOUT THE END RESULT — THAT PEOPLE SHOULD FOLLOW THE LAW, FROM WHATEVER MOTIVE — WHICH WAS PRECISELY THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT INTERESTED CONFUCIUS.

cards.q: How did Confucianism and Legalism differ in their view of punishment?
cards.a: On human nature and on what matters. Confucians: people are born good, order is held by MORAL FORCES — orders and punishments deter wrongdoing but do not teach shame. Legalists: nature is inherently bad because of bodily desires, LAW AND PUNISHMENT decide — and what they care about is the END RESULT, that people follow the law FROM WHATEVER MOTIVE.

6.title: The division of roles that lasted two thousand years
6.text: Legalism was adopted as the guiding policy of the state of QIN, which helped it conquer the six other states and found the QIN dynasty (221–206 BC), THE FIRST IMPERIAL STATE IN CHINA. It was short-lived, however, and the HAN which replaced it wanted to learn from its predecessor's rapid fall. The first three Han emperors favoured DAOISM, but the fourth, Emperor WU, was persuaded by the Confucian scholar DONG ZHONGSHU to adopt CONFUCIANISM AS THE OFFICIAL IDEOLOGY. This established the predominance of Confucianism in the Chinese tradition once and for all. BUT LEGALISM WAS BY NO MEANS ABANDONED — and this is the key formula: FROM THE HAN DYNASTY ONWARDS EVERY SUCCEEDING DYNASTY USED CONFUCIAN IDEOLOGY FOR MORAL PRINCIPLES AND LEGALIST PRACTICES AS TOOLS OF GOVERNANCE, because both were indispensable to a ruler. The HISTORY OF THE YUAN puts it this way: 'WHOEVER RULES ALL UNDER HEAVEN, EVEN WERE THEY WISE EMPERORS, CANNOT ACHIEVE GOOD GOVERNANCE WITHOUT LAW AND PUNISHMENT… THE FORMER RULERS MADE LAW AND PUNISHMENT NOT TO ESTABLISH AUTHORITY BUT TO ASSIST GOOD GOVERNANCE.' In short: CONFUCIANISM AS THE PREVAILING IDEOLOGY JUSTIFIED THE ORDER, WHILE LAW AND PUNISHMENT AS TOOLS INFORMED BY LEGALISM ENFORCED IT.

cards.q: How did Confucianism and Legalism divide the roles between them in imperial China?
cards.a: CONFUCIANISM as the prevailing ideology JUSTIFIED the political-social-moral ORDER; LAW AND PUNISHMENT as tools of governance informed by LEGALISM ENFORCED it. From the Han dynasty onwards every succeeding dynasty did it this way — both were indispensable to a ruler.

7.title: Fu Su: why the family is the heart of the matter
7.text: The story Xu uses as the key. In 210 BC the First Emperor of the Qin died while travelling. The chief eunuch ZHAO GAO concealed his death and persuaded the counsellor LI SI that the throne should pass to the younger son HU HAI, who would be easier to control. To forestall trouble they FORGED, IN THE DEAD EMPEROR'S NAME, AN ORDER to Hu Hai's elder brother FU SU and to General MENG TIAN, both at the Great Wall, TO COMMIT SUICIDE. Meng was suspicious and urged that they demand an explanation. FU SU REPLIED: 'IF A FATHER ASKS HIS SON TO DIE, THERE IS NO NEED TO ASK FOR ANYTHING FURTHER.' AND HE KILLED HIMSELF. This brings us to the core: the moral implications of the patriarchal family and its ideology of FILIAL PIETY can be summed up as follows. THE INDIVIDUAL IS INSIGNIFICANT EXCEPT AS A MEMBER OF A FAMILY; he is NEITHER MORE NOR LESS THAN A LINK IN THE CHAIN OF THE PATRIARCHAL LINEAGE connecting ancestors and descendants, and CONTINUING THE LINEAGE IS A MAN'S FOREMOST MORAL DUTY; WOMEN ARE INDISPENSABLE FOR REPRODUCING THE LINEAGE BUT SUBORDINATE AND SUBJECT TO MEN, JUST AS YIN IS TO YANG; and finally IT IS ESSENTIAL THAT CHILDREN COMPLETELY OBEY AND HONOUR PARENTS, GRANDPARENTS AND OTHER ELDERS — AS FU SU DID. And the bridge to politics: THE STATE WAS SIMPLY UNDERSTOOD AS A PATRIARCHAL FAMILY WRIT LARGE — the ruler was Son of Heaven and parent of the people at once.

terms.def: Complete obedience to and reverence for parents and elders; because the state is 'a patriarchal family writ large', it is at the same time a political virtue.

cards.q: Why did Fu Su kill himself on an order his own general doubted?
cards.a: Because the order came in the name of his FATHER: 'If a father asks his son to die, there is no need to ask for anything further.' The story shows the force of the ideology of FILIAL PIETY — and because the state was understood as a patriarchal family writ large and the ruler was the parent of the people, obedience to a father was a political virtue as well.

cards.q: Sum up the moral implications of the patriarchal family in four points.
cards.a: The individual is insignificant except as a member of a family; he is a link in the chain of the lineage between ancestors and descendants, and CONTINUING THE LINEAGE is a man's foremost moral duty; women are indispensable for reproducing the lineage but subordinate to men as yin is to yang; and children must completely obey and honour parents, grandparents and elders.

8.title: The Five Punishments and the first written laws
8.text: The 'BOOK OF YU: THE CANON OF SHUN' in the CLASSIC OF DOCUMENTS vaguely mentions the 'FIVE PUNISHMENTS' and refers to DECAPITATION AND MUTILATIONS. Whether they were already used under Shun was later disputed; more probably they were used in some form under the Xia, and certainly under the Shang and Zhou, as archaeological finds and written sources show. During the SPRING AND AUTUMN period (770–476 BC), when the earlier fiefs developed into independent feudal states, 'WRITTEN' LAWS began to appear: several states PUBLISHED THEIR BASIC PENAL CODES INSCRIBED ON BRONZE OR IRON STRUCTURES. Of far-reaching influence were the CANON OF LAWS (FAJING) compiled by LI KUI of the state of Wei. They have not survived, but the citations show that they had SIX BOOKS: ROBBERY AND THEFT, REBELLION, DETENTION, ARREST, MISCELLANEOUS OFFENCES (gambling, fraud, bribes, climbing walls, illicit sex) AND GENERAL PRINCIPLES — these categories remained central to the penal codes of the whole imperial era. And two principles already present here: THE LEGISLATORS OF THE ZHOU PERIOD ALREADY DISTINGUISHED INTENTIONAL FROM UNINTENTIONAL OFFENCES AND REPEAT OFFENDERS FROM FIRST OFFENDERS, the latter being punished more leniently. Early punishments included the DEATH PENALTY, BODILY MUTILATIONS, TATTOOING AND ENSLAVEMENT; less regular were BANISHMENT, WHIPPING, BEATING AND FINES (by which mutilation and tattooing could be redeemed where guilt was less conclusive).

cards.q: What did the Canon of Laws (Fajing) contain and why does it matter?
cards.a: Six books: robbery and theft, rebellion, detention, arrest, miscellaneous offences (gambling, fraud, bribes, illicit sex) and general principles. It matters because THESE CATEGORIES REMAINED CENTRAL to the penal codes of the entire imperial era — even though the Canon itself has not survived and is known only from citations.

cards.q: Which legal principles already existed in the Zhou period?
cards.a: The distinction between INTENTIONAL and UNINTENTIONAL offences and between REPEAT OFFENDERS and FIRST OFFENDERS, first offenders being punished more leniently. And the redemption of mutilation and tattooing by a FINE where guilt was less conclusive.

9.title: Qin: Shang Yang and the equality that backfired
9.text: The success of the state of Qin was owed to the Legalist approach of SHANG YANG, who came from neighbouring Wei and became chief counsellor. He recommended HARSH LAWS AND SEVERE PUNISHMENTS to achieve the state's goals, advised the EQUAL APPLICATION OF LAW AND PUNISHMENT TO ALL MEMBERS OF SOCIETY, and introduced a SYSTEM OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY OF EVERY TEN FAMILIES IN A NEIGHBOURHOOD for crimes committed there. His insistence on equality before the law led to a case in which the CROWN PRINCE committed an offence and HIS TWO TUTORS WERE PUNISHED IN HIS PLACE. When the prince came to the throne he sought revenge and ordered Shang's arrest for sedition. According to the historian SIMA QIAN, Shang fled for his life, stopped at an inn for food and water — AND THE OWNER, NOT KNOWING WHO HE WAS TALKING TO, SAID THAT UNDER THE LAW ISSUED BY LORD SHANG HE WOULD BE PUNISHED IF HE SERVED ANYONE WITHOUT PROOF OF IDENTITY. SHANG SIGHED AT HIS OWN HARSH LAW. In the end he was forced into actual rebellion and was hideously executed. One lasting innovation remained from Qin law: PENAL LABOUR, often imposed together with tattooing or mutilation — men most often on the construction of palaces, tombs, walls, roads and the Great Wall, or transporting goods and serving at the frontier, women as slaves or servants of the state. The bamboo strips excavated in 1975 at YUNMENG contain laws on agriculture, taxes, labour services, currency and markets, storehouses, rewards and appointments, and also MODEL LEGAL DOCUMENTS AND PROCEDURES OF INVESTIGATION, INTERROGATION AND TRIAL.

cards.q: What did Shang Yang introduce and how did he end?
cards.a: Harsh laws and severe punishments, the EQUAL application of law to all members of society, and COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY of every ten families in a neighbourhood. When the crown prince committed an offence, his two tutors were punished in his place — and the prince, on coming to the throne, had Shang prosecuted. In flight, an innkeeper refused to serve him without proof of identity under Shang's own law; in the end he was hideously executed.

cards.q: What lasting innovation came with Qin law?
cards.a: PENAL LABOUR, often imposed together with tattooing or mutilation: men on the construction of palaces, tombs, walls, roads and the Great Wall, or transporting goods and serving at the frontier; women as slaves or servants of the state.

10.title: Han: the reform of punishments that could kill more
10.text: Soon after the founding of the Han came the LAW IN NINE CHAPTERS — the first six after the old Canon of Laws, three new ones after Qin models. The Han then grew by way of articles added to the code (LÜ), imperial edicts (LING), adjustments of particulars (KE) and judicial precedents or analogies (BI). For punishments the old five-part scheme applied UNTIL 167 BC, when Emperor WEN reformed it: he replaced TATTOOING with PENAL LABOUR, the CUTTING OFF OF THE NOSE AND THE LEFT TOE with BEATING, and the cutting off of the RIGHT TOE with DECAPITATION. And here is the trap worth knowing: THE SPIRIT OF THE REFORM WAS TO ABOLISH MUTILATION, BUT TWO SENIOR OFFICIALS REMARKED AT THE TIME THAT THE CHANGE WOULD SOFTEN PUNISHMENTS ONLY IN APPEARANCE AND WOULD IN FACT INCREASE THE NUMBER OF EXECUTIONS. In 156 BC, accordingly, Emperor JING, responding to reports that many who had been spared the death penalty HAD NONETHELESS DIED OF THE BEATING, reduced five hundred strokes to three hundred; twelve years later three hundred to two hundred and two hundred to one hundred, and THE INSTRUMENTS OF BEATING WERE STANDARDISED. These changes were a TURNING POINT in the Chinese conception of punishment and set in motion the move away from bodily mutilation. A further change: in Qin, penal labour was FOR LIFE; the Han began to FIX ITS TERM — the heaviest was construction work with a shaved head and in chains (for women, husking rice) for five years, the lightest general labour or frontier guard duty, and for women menial palace work, for one year. And CASTRATION: it was not in the early Han code; Emperor Jing added it; it was inflicted on the court historian SIMA QIAN for defending a general who had surrendered to the Xiongnu without supplies. In the late Han castration was abolished again.

cards.q: What did Emperor Wen's reform of punishments in 167 BC do, and what was the objection?
cards.a: It replaced tattooing with penal labour, the cutting off of the nose and the left toe with beating, and the cutting off of the right toe with DECAPITATION. The objection of two senior officials was that the change would soften punishments ONLY IN APPEARANCE AND WOULD IN FACT INCREASE THE NUMBER OF EXECUTIONS — and Emperor Jing did indeed have to reduce the number of strokes, because many who had been spared death were dying of the beating.

cards.q: How did penal labour change in the Han compared with Qin?
cards.a: In Qin it was FOR LIFE; the Han began to fix its TERM — from the heaviest (construction work with a shaved head and in chains, for women husking rice) at five years, down to the lightest (general labour or frontier guard duty, for women menial palace work) at one year.

cards.q: Why were officials punished more severely than commoners?
cards.a: Because of what modern scholarship calls the PRINCIPAL-AGENT RELATIONSHIP: the ruler must monitor, at a cost, officials who tend to act against his interests. Han Fei described it as a conflict of interest — the king wants capable ministers, ministers want income without capability; the king wants to reward work, ministers want wealth without work. From Emperor Wu onwards categories of offence applicable only to officials and members of the imperial clan were created.

11.title: The period of division: why law matured precisely then
11.text: After the end of the Han in 220 came almost FOUR CENTURIES OF POLITICAL DIVISION — the Three Kingdoms, the Jin, sixteen states in the north, four short dynasties in the south — until the Sui reunified the country in 589. And Xu shows why this was fruitful for law: EVERY COMPETING STATE OR SHORT DYNASTY REGARDED A NEW PENAL CODE AS A WAY OF SYMBOLISING A NEW AND BETTER GOVERNMENT WITH THE MANDATE OF HEAVEN. The result was that Chinese law entered a PHASE OF MATURATION. The codes at the same time expressed MORE THAN EVER BEFORE the Confucian concerns with the patriarchal family and the absolute power of the emperor — and this despite (or precisely because of) the growing influence of Buddhism and religious Daoism. The reason is institutional: THE LEGISLATORS IN THESE STATES, INCLUDING THOSE FOUNDED BY NOMADS, WERE CONFUCIAN SCHOLARS WHO FACILITATED THE SINICISATION OF NOMADIC PEOPLES. The most important work was the CODE OF WEI (220–265) with EIGHTEEN CHAPTERS, which MOVED THE CHAPTER ON LEGAL PRINCIPLES TO FIRST PLACE — as against the Han Law in Nine Chapters, which treated principles in the last. The CODE OF JIN (266–316) had TWENTY CHAPTERS AND 1,530 ARTICLES. To it the judicial official ZHANG FEI wrote a preface which defined the concepts: how to assess an offence as intentional, unintentional or negligent; what constitutes fraud, assault, an unfilial act; how to distinguish INITIATING A CRIME, CONSPIRING IN IT AND LEADING A GROUP IN COMMITTING IT; how to punish an offender of multiple crimes. This created a USEFUL FRAMEWORK OF LEGAL THEORY for later legislators.

cards.q: Why did four centuries of division bring a flowering of penal legislation?
cards.a: Because EVERY competing state or short dynasty regarded a NEW PENAL CODE AS A WAY OF SYMBOLISING A NEW AND BETTER GOVERNMENT WITH THE MANDATE OF HEAVEN. Chinese law thereby entered its phase of maturation, and much of what was developed then was inherited by the great dynasties.

cards.q: Why did the Confucian emphases in the codes deepen even in states founded by nomads?
cards.a: Because THE LEGISLATORS EVEN IN THOSE STATES WERE CONFUCIAN SCHOLARS, who facilitated the SINICISATION of the nomadic peoples. Confucianism thus operated through the personnel of the administration regardless of the ruler's ethnic origin.

12.title: The Eight Deliberations and the Ten Abominations
12.text: Two institutions which from then on belonged in every major code. The EIGHT DELIBERATIONS (BAYI) entered a code for the first time in the CODE OF WEI (220–265), although the notion is older. They were EIGHT CATEGORIES OF PERSONS FOR WHOM LENIENCY WAS TO BE CONSIDERED IN SENTENCING: THE EMPEROR'S RELATIVES, THE EMPEROR'S FRIENDS, HIGHLY ESTEEMED PERSONS, HIGHLY CAPABLE PERSONS, HIGHLY MERITORIOUS PERSONS, HIGH OFFICIALS, HIGHLY DILIGENT PERSONS AND THE IMPERIAL DESCENDANTS OF PREVIOUS DYNASTIES. This privileged the imperial clan and the aristocracy, but it also treated the TALENTED more leniently so as to serve the interest of the state — and how 'capable', 'meritorious' and 'diligent' were defined WAS LEFT TO THE DISCRETION OF THE JUDICIAL OFFICIALS. The TEN ABOMINATIONS (SHI'E) appeared first in the code of the NORTHERN QI: ten types of the most abominable crimes, deserving the severest punishments and WHICH COULD NOT BE REDEEMED BY A FINE, MITIGATED BY THE EIGHT DELIBERATIONS OR COVERED BY AN IMPERIAL AMNESTY. They were: 1) PLOTTING REBELLION, 2) PLOTTING SEDITIOUS ACTS (destroying imperial temples, tombs and the palace), 3) PLOTTING TREASON, 4) UNFILIAL EVIL ACTS (beating or killing parents, grandparents and other close kin), 5) DEPRAVITY (killing three people of one family, killing by dismemberment, poisoning or black magic), 6) GREAT IRREVERENCE (stealing or forging imperial robes and objects, failure in service to the emperor, insulting the emperor), 7) UNFILIAL CONDUCT (accusing or insulting parents, taking family property, marrying during mourning, failing to observe mourning, falsely reporting a parent's death), 8) DISCORDANT CONDUCT (killing or selling senior relatives), 9) UNRIGHTEOUS CONDUCT (killing local officials, teachers or officials of the fifth rank and above, failing to observe mourning for a husband), 10) INCEST. And the interpretation: THE TEN ABOMINATIONS WERE EVIDENTLY DESIGNED ABOVE ALL TO PROTECT THE PATRIARCHAL FAMILY AND THE POSITION OF THE EMPEROR AS SON OF HEAVEN AND PARENT OF THE PEOPLE — and note that rebellion against the emperor and beating one's parents stand in the same list.

terms.def: Eight categories of persons for whom leniency in punishment was to be considered — from the emperor's relatives and friends to highly capable and diligent persons.
The ten gravest crimes, not redeemable by fine, not mitigable by the Eight Deliberations and not covered by amnesty — protecting the emperor and the patriarchal family at once.

cards.q: What are the Eight Deliberations and what are the Ten Abominations, and how are they connected?
cards.a: The EIGHT DELIBERATIONS are eight categories of persons for whom LENIENCY was considered (the emperor's relatives and friends, the esteemed, the capable, the meritorious, high officials, the diligent, descendants of previous dynasties). The TEN ABOMINATIONS are the ten gravest crimes, which could NOT be redeemed by a fine, mitigated by the Eight Deliberations or covered by an amnesty. They are thus each other's counterpoint: both entered the codes in the period of division and remained the standard.

cards.q: What does the list of Ten Abominations show about the values of Chinese law?
cards.a: That it protects TWO THINGS AS ONE: the position of the emperor as Son of Heaven and parent of the people (rebellion, sedition, treason, great irreverence) and the patriarchal family (unfilial evil acts, unfilial conduct, discord, unrighteous conduct, incest). Rebellion against the emperor and beating one's parents stand in the same list.

cards.q: How were old and young offenders treated?
cards.a: The classical sources already stated that the old and the weak should not be punished; the 'Rites of Zhou' ranked amnesty first for the young and weak, then the old, then the mentally disabled. Under the Han the principle became firmly established, and it became usual that PERSONS OF SEVENTY AND ABOVE AND MINORS UNDER TEN WERE NOT LIABLE FOR ANY OFFENCE EXCEPT TREASON AND MURDER.

13.title: The new Five Punishments and redemption by office
13.text: During the period of division punishments shifted FROM THE OLD FIVE PUNISHMENTS OF BODILY MUTILATION TO THE NEW FIVE PUNISHMENTS: DEATH; BANISHMENT WITH BEATING; PENAL LABOUR WITH WHIPPING OR BEATING; WHIPPING; AND BEATING. In mitigating circumstances they could be redeemed by a FINE — the code of the NORTHERN ZHOU even fixed deadlines for the families of the condemned to raise the money, FROM FIFTY DAYS FOR THE DEATH PENALTY DOWN TO TEN DAYS FOR BEATING, and 'THE VERY POOR MAY APPLY FOR EXEMPTION FROM PAYMENT'. The SUI code (589–617), largely modelled on the Northern Qi, then SIMPLIFIED the system into TWELVE BOOKS AND FIVE HUNDRED ARTICLES, REDUCED THE NUMBER OF OFFENCES PUNISHED BY DEATH, BANISHMENT AND PENAL LABOUR, and ABOLISHED some cruel punishments — DISMEMBERMENT, THE DISPLAY OF A SEVERED HEAD AND THE ENSLAVEMENT OF FAMILY MEMBERS. The Five Punishments received their precise form: DEATH (strangulation or decapitation); BANISHMENT (1,000, 1,500 or 2,000 LI); PENAL LABOUR (one to three years in five degrees); BEATING (60 to 100 strokes in five degrees), which replaced whipping; and LIGHT BEATING (10 to 50 strokes in five degrees). And an innovation arrived which reveals the whole character of the system: REDEMPTION OF PUNISHMENT BY OFFICE — officials of the seventh rank and above convicted of an offence received a REDUCTION OF ONE DEGREE, those of the fifth rank and above could deduct TWO YEARS of penal labour, those of the ninth to sixth rank ONE YEAR. Xu draws the conclusion directly: THE CONFUCIAN ORDER DID NOT REST ON THE PRINCIPLE OF EQUALITY BUT ON HIERARCHY, AND NEITHER DID THE PENAL CODES REST ON THE IDEA OF EQUALITY BEFORE THE LAW — SHANG YANG'S LEGALIST APPROACH WAS LOST IN FAVOUR OF THE CONFUCIAN CONCEPTION OF HIERARCHY. Hierarchy nevertheless cut both ways: HIGHER STANDARDS OF CONDUCT APPLIED TO OFFICIALS, since some articles and special regulations applied to them alone.

cards.q: Name the 'new Five Punishments' as they settled by the Sui period.
cards.a: Death (strangulation or decapitation); banishment (1,000, 1,500 or 2,000 li) with beating; penal labour (one to three years in five degrees) with whipping or beating; beating (60–100 strokes in five degrees); and light beating (10–50 strokes in five degrees). They replaced the old five punishments of bodily mutilation.

cards.q: What is redemption of punishment by office, and what does it prove?
cards.a: Officials of the seventh rank and above convicted of an offence received a reduction of one degree, those of the fifth and above could deduct two years of penal labour, those of the ninth to sixth one year. It proves that THE CONFUCIAN ORDER RESTED NOT ON EQUALITY BUT ON HIERARCHY — Shang Yang's Legalist approach of equality before the law was lost. Hierarchy did, however, cut both ways: higher standards of conduct applied to officials.

14.title: The Tang Code: the summit and the model
14.text: THE TANG CODE WITH COMMENTARIES (TANGLÜ SHUYI) was promulgated in 653 and is a LANDMARK OF CHINESE LEGAL HISTORY for three reasons. FIRST, it was the CULMINATION OF ALL PREVIOUS LEGISLATION from the pre-imperial period, with maturity and clarity of concepts, built on the moral and practical deliberations of more than a millennium. SECOND, it was the FIRST CHINESE PENAL CODE TO SURVIVE IN ITS ENTIRETY through several dynasties into modern times, and it served as the MODEL OF THE SUCCEEDING IMPERIAL CODES. THIRD, it had a WIDE INFLUENCE ON LEGAL DEVELOPMENT IN NEIGHBOURING COUNTRIES — IN JAPAN, KOREA AND VIETNAM. It had THIRTY CHAPTERS AND 502 ARTICLES and covered twelve broad fields: legal principles (the five punishments, the ten abominations, the eight deliberations, redemption by office, voluntary confession, exemption from punishment for the aged, minors and the sick or disabled), the imperial guard and prohibitions, administrative regulations, household and marriage, public stables and storehouses, unauthorised levies, violence and robbery, assault and accusation, fraud and forgery, miscellaneous articles, arrest and escape, and judgment and prison. At the urging of Emperor TAIZONG the death penalty for the brothers of an offender convicted of treason (collective punishment) was changed to BANISHMENT, which led to a wider revision: THE DEATH PENALTY FOR 92 OFFENCES UNDER THE SUI CODE WAS CHANGED TO BANISHMENT AND BANISHMENT FOR 71 OFFENCES TO PENAL LABOUR.

cards.q: Why is the Tang Code of 653 a landmark? Give three reasons.
cards.a: 1) It was the CULMINATION of all previous legislation from the pre-imperial period, with maturity and clarity of concepts. 2) It was the FIRST Chinese penal code to survive IN ITS ENTIRETY, and became the MODEL of those that followed. 3) It widely influenced legal development in JAPAN, KOREA AND VIETNAM.

cards.q: What shift in severity did the Tang Code bring compared with the Sui code?
cards.a: The death penalty for 92 offences was changed to banishment and banishment for 71 offences to penal labour. The impulse was Emperor Taizong's decision to change the collective death penalty for the brothers of a traitor to banishment.

15.title: Article 48: Chinese legal pluralism
15.text: The Tang Code was THE FIRST TO WRITE DOWN EXPLICITLY WHAT IN CHINESE HISTORY IS CALLED 'LEGAL PLURALISM'. ARTICLE 48: IF VARIOUS 'UNCIVILISED PEOPLES' (HUAWAI REN, literally people outside Chinese civilisation) COMMIT OFFENCES WITHIN THEIR OWN GROUPS, THEIR CUSTOMARY RULES (SUFA) APPLY; IF THEY COMMIT THEM BETWEEN GROUPS, THE LAW OF THE TANG DYNASTY (FALÜ) APPLIES. The commentary made it precise: 'uncivilised peoples' are those in non-Chinese states which have set up their own rulers, each with their own mores, customs and institutions; if it happened within such a state, it is settled according to its institutions and customs — if it happened BETWEEN TWO PEOPLES, say GOGURYEO AND BAEKJE (two Korean states then at war with one another), TANG STATE LAW (GUOJIA FALÜ) decides. That example is telling in itself: IT REFLECTS THE IDEA OF CHINESE SUPREMACY OVER THE KOREAN RULERS. And the cause of this pluralism is demographic: a diverse population under the Tang state after centuries of migration of non-Chinese peoples into northern China and of Chinese to the south, and a growing number of foreigners residing in China — THE TANG STATE ADAPTED LAW AND JUSTICE TO THAT DEMOGRAPHIC REALITY.

terms.def: 'People outside Chinese civilisation'. Under art. 48 of the Tang Code their customary law applied to offences within their group, Tang law to offences between groups.

cards.q: What did article 48 of the Tang Code provide?
cards.a: That if 'uncivilised peoples' (huawai ren) commit offences WITHIN their own groups, their CUSTOMARY rules (sufa) apply; if they commit them BETWEEN groups, TANG law (falü) applies. It is the first explicit writing-down of Chinese legal pluralism — and its cause was the demographic diversity created by centuries of migration.

16.title: Song: the code that fell out of use
16.text: The Song code was compiled within three years of the founding of the dynasty, in content following the Tang, but with a NEW FORMAT: the structure of thirty books remained, but to the individual articles were attached COMMENTARIES (SHU), EDICTS (GE), REGULATIONS (LING), ADJUSTMENTS (SHI) AND DIRECTIVES (CHI) on the same matter. And then the important consequence: THE SONG WENT ON COMPILING LEGAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE DIRECTIVES (CHI) AND PRECEDENTS (LI) ARISING IN EVERYDAY GOVERNANCE, SO THAT OFFICIALS BEGAN TO DECIDE BY THE DIRECTIVES AND PRECEDENTS RATHER THAN BY THE CODE. Law and punishment in the Song also RETREATED in several respects from the earlier trend towards mitigation: TATTOOING was restored as a supplementary punishment (for those sentenced to banishment and penal labour), and so was SLICING TO DEATH as one of the forms of the death penalty for grave crimes. Under Emperor SHENZONG the LAW ON THE SEVERE PUNISHMENT OF ROBBERY AND REBELLION (DAOZEI ZHONGFA) was enacted: in any area designated by the central government as one with active robbers and rebels, THIS SPECIAL LAW with harsher punishments applied instead of the relevant articles of the code — the family property of a person sentenced to death was confiscated to reward informers and his wife was banished 1,000 li. IN THE END A LARGE PART OF THE COUNTRY BECAME AN AREA WHERE THAT SPECIAL LAW APPLIED — which points to the spread of peasant rebellions born of poverty and desperation despite general economic growth, commercialisation and urbanisation.

cards.q: What happened to the standing of the code in practice under the Song?
cards.a: The Song went on compiling LEGAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE DIRECTIVES (chi) and PRECEDENTS (li) arising in everyday governance, so that OFFICIALS BEGAN TO DECIDE BY THEM RATHER THAN BY THE CODE. The same thing happened later in the Ming with the sub-statutes (li).

cards.q: In what way did the Song retreat from the mitigation of punishments?
cards.a: It restored TATTOOING as a supplementary punishment and SLICING TO DEATH as a form of the death penalty. And under Emperor Shenzong it enacted the LAW ON THE SEVERE PUNISHMENT OF ROBBERY AND REBELLION, which in designated areas replaced the code with harsher punishments — and in the end its reach extended over a large part of the country.

17.title: Yuan: ethnic hierarchy and two unintended legacies
17.text: The Mongols ruled China AS A CONQUERED COUNTRY and had no intention of assimilating into Chinese society. Unlike the previous dynasties, therefore, YUAN RULE RESTED ON AN ETHNIC HIERARCHY INSTEAD OF A SOCIAL ONE: the population was divided into four ranks — MONGOLS, ALLIED NOMADIC PEOPLES, NORTHERN CHINESE, SOUTHERN CHINESE (conquered last) — and THE CHINESE WERE PUNISHED MORE SEVERELY THAN THE MONGOLS FOR THE SAME OFFENCE. The Yuan code of 1323 was a HYBRID of the Chinese tradition and Mongol practice: twenty books and 2,539 articles in three categories — EDICTS (ZHAOZHI), STATUTES (TIAOGE) AND PRECEDENTS (DUANLI). Punishments were somewhat LIGHTER than before; the death penalty was carried out by DECAPITATION or, for treason, by SLICING, and STRANGULATION WAS ABOLISHED. Ming scholars noted in the History of the Yuan that all dynasties issued amnesties, BUT THAT ONLY IN THE YUAN WERE THERE AMNESTIES ON ACCOUNT OF BUDDHIST FESTIVALS (the Mongols had adopted Tibetan Buddhism). And two unintended legacies. FIRST: in 1315 the Yuan restored the CIVIL SERVICE EXAMINATIONS and issued an abridged curriculum based on the FOUR BOOKS compiled by the Neo-Confucian ZHU XI — and that curriculum became the core of the examinations in the Ming and the Qing. SECOND: in 1314 five brothers were sentenced to death and Emperor RENZONG sighed: 'IT IS A MISFORTUNE THAT THIS HAPPENED TO THIS FAMILY; CHOOSE THE ONE WHO WAS LEAST GUILTY, PUNISH HIM WITH A BEATING AND LET HIM SUPPORT HIS PARENTS, SO THAT THE FAMILY DOES NOT END ITS LINE.' He thereby revived the long-lost NORTHERN WEI principle 'ONE IS SPARED FROM DEATH TO SUPPORT THE PARENTS' (LIUCUN YANGQIN), which then entered the Ming and Qing codes. And Xu's comment: IT IS INSTRUCTIVE THAT THE PRINCIPLE WAS FIRST PROPOSED BY A XIANBEI AND THEN REVIVED BY A MONGOL RULER — both NON-CHINESE — before it became established in the Chinese codes.

terms.def: 'One is spared from death to support the parents' — a principle preserving the family line; proposed by the Northern Wei, revived by the Mongol emperor Renzong in 1314.

cards.q: What did Yuan rule rest on, and how did that show in punishment?
cards.a: On an ETHNIC hierarchy instead of a social one: four ranks — Mongols, allied nomadic peoples, northern Chinese, southern Chinese — and THE CHINESE WERE PUNISHED MORE SEVERELY THAN THE MONGOLS FOR THE SAME OFFENCE.

cards.q: What is the principle of liucun yangqin and why is it instructive who established it?
cards.a: 'One is spared from death to support the parents' — so that the family does not end its line. It appeared first under the Northern Wei, was revived in 1314 by the Mongol emperor Renzong, and from there entered the Ming and Qing codes. What is instructive is that it was proposed by a Xianbei and revived by a Mongol — both NON-CHINESE — which says something about the acculturating effect of Confucianism.

18.title: Ming: seven categories and the sub-statutes
18.text: THE GREAT MING CODE was produced in 1374 and took its final form in 1397 — before that ZHU YUANZHANG had, a year before proclaiming himself emperor, had a provisional code of 285 articles drawn up, again as a symbol of the new dynasty's Mandate of Heaven. It largely followed the Tang model, but with novelties: THIRTY BOOKS AND 460 ARTICLES, arranged in SEVEN CATEGORIES — PRINCIPLES; PERSONNEL; HOUSEHOLD (population registers, labour services, land and housing, marriage, harvest and the grain tax, commercial tax, money and debts, markets); RITES; THE MILITARY SYSTEM (palace security, military administration, passes and ferries, stables and pasture, the transmission of messages); PUNISHMENTS (robbery and theft, homicide, assault, insults, litigation, bribes, fraud, illicit sex, miscellaneous offences, the capture of fugitives, judgment); and PUBLIC WORKS (construction and waterworks). The Ming code thus took a FURTHER STEP IN THE RATIONALISATION AND SYSTEMATISATION of legal categories. In 1500 the SUB-STATUTES FOR ADJUDICATION (WENXING TIAOLI) were compiled — a collection supplementing or altering the articles of the code and giving guidance for circumstances the code did not enumerate; it was issued separately at first and later the sub-statutes were attached to the relevant articles. AND THE SAME THING AGAIN: OFFICIALS DECIDED BY THE SUB-STATUTES RATHER THAN BY THE ARTICLES OF THE CODE. On ethnic minorities: the code said that the law applied UNIFORMLY to non-Chinese (huawai ren) as well, BUT a sub-statute of 1436 for the natives of GUIZHOU province mitigated punishments — the death penalty to lifelong penal labour, banishment or penal labour with beating to mere penal labour, beating to ten months' labour and light beating to five — EVIDENTLY BECAUSE THE MINORITIES WERE NOT ASSIMILATED INTO CHINESE CULTURE AND DID NOT KNOW CHINESE LAW.

cards.q: How was the Great Ming Code arranged?
cards.a: Thirty books and 460 articles in SEVEN categories: principles; personnel; household; rites; the military system; punishments; and public works. It largely followed the Tang model and took a further step in the rationalisation and systematisation of legal categories.

cards.q: Why were punishments mitigated for the natives of Guizhou under the Ming, when the code proclaimed the uniform application of law?
cards.a: Because they were not assimilated into Chinese culture and DID NOT KNOW CHINESE LAW. The sub-statute of 1436 changed the death penalty to lifelong penal labour, banishment or labour with beating to mere labour, beating to ten months' labour and light beating to five.

19.title: Qing: the culmination and the multi-ethnic empire
19.text: Unlike the Mongols, the Manchus INTENDED TO ASSIMILATE FULLY INTO CHINESE SOCIETY AND CULTURE in order to govern effectively — while preserving their own Manchu identity by practices such as NOT INTERMARRYING WITH HAN CHINESE AND PROHIBITING FOOT-BINDING FOR MANCHU WOMEN. Emperor QIANLONG wrote a preface to the code in 1740 in which he derived the origins of legislation from the sage-kings of the Classic of Documents: 'MY IMPERIAL ANCESTORS RECEIVED THE CLEAR MANDATE OF HEAVEN TO PACIFY AND GOVERN ALL THE LANDS, AND ISSUED THE GREAT QING CODE AND SUB-STATUTES SO THAT BENEVOLENCE, EDUCATION, JUSTICE AND CORRECTION SHOULD BE IN THEIR PROPER PLACES.' The first version, on the Ming model, was produced in 1646, revised in 1727, and given its final form in 1740: THIRTY BOOKS, THE SAME SEVEN CATEGORIES, 436 ARTICLES (24 fewer than the Ming). The number of SUB-STATUTES, however, kept growing: TO 824 BY 1727, TO OVER 1,400 BY 1740 AND TO 1,892 BY 1870. Alongside the code the Board of Punishments compiled CASE COLLECTIONS: the most influential was the CONSPECTUS OF PENAL CASES (XING'AN HUILAN) with over 5,600 cases from 1736–1834 (plus over 300 from 1842–1885); further, the COLLECTION OF CORRECTED CASES with 379 cases personally reviewed by emperors; and the COLLECTION OF CASES OF AGGRAVATION AND MITIGATION BY ANALOGY with 2,992 cases from 1843. These collections SERVED AS LEGAL INTERPRETATIONS AND PRECEDENTS and were genuinely used in adjudication. To these were added REGULATIONS ISSUED BY PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES AND APPROVED BY THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT — the outcome of negotiation between the Board of Punishments and the emperor on one side and the provincial governors on the other about how better to apply the law to conditions the code did not cover.

cards.q: How did the sub-statutes grow in the Qing, and what does that say about the nature of the code?
cards.a: To 824 items by 1727, to over 1,400 by 1740 and to 1,892 by 1870 — while the code itself had 436 articles. The code alone therefore did not suffice for adjudication; the real law lay in the sub-statutes, the case collections (the Conspectus of Penal Cases with over 5,600 cases) and the provincial regulations.

cards.q: How did the Manchus differ from the Mongols in their relation to Chinese culture?
cards.a: They INTENDED TO ASSIMILATE FULLY into Chinese society and culture in order to govern effectively — they adopted the Mandate of Heaven and the Confucian tradition — while keeping their Manchu identity through practices such as not intermarrying with Han Chinese and prohibiting foot-binding for Manchu women. The Mongols, by contrast, ruled China as a conquered country and did not wish to assimilate.

20.title: Qing legal pluralism of a multi-ethnic empire
20.text: The Manchus RECONCEIVED CHINA, IN A HISTORICALLY SIGNIFICANT WAY, AS A MULTI-ETHNIC ENTITY RATHER THAN A PURELY CHINESE ONE. Into their territory they incorporated what previous dynasties had regarded as frontier regions contested with nomads — MANCHURIA, MONGOLIA, XINJIANG AND TIBET — plus the island of TAIWAN, and thereby defined what has since been regarded as China in modern times. To administer those regions they established the COURT OF COLONIAL AFFAIRS (LIFAN YUAN) and practised LEGAL PLURALISM: under the code the law still applied to non-Chinese (huawai ren), but those administered by that office were governed by the MONGOL STATUTES (MENGGU LI). Other localised laws existed as well: in XINJIANG the SINO-MUSLIM REGIONAL STATUTES (HUIJIANG ZELI) applied, as did the statutes of the office itself. CRIMINAL CASES AMONG MONGOLS, TIBETANS, UYGHURS, KAZAKHS AND OTHERS WERE DECIDED ACCORDING TO THEIR OWN INDIGENOUS LAWS AND CIVIL DISPUTES ACCORDING TO LOCAL CUSTOM — the sources included ISLAMIC LAW and ethnic traditions. Manchu soldiers, the so-called BANNERMEN, kept separate from Chinese units, were subject to a SPECIAL PENAL CODE. And there were exceptions in the form of special sub-statutes for frontier regions or for the metropolitan areas of Beijing and Shenyang — either to make punishments HARSHER (in Beijing and Shenyang) or to make procedure and punishment MORE FLEXIBLE (on the frontier). The difference from the Ming lies in scale and in perspective: QING POLICY WAS CARRIED OUT ON A MUCH LARGER SCALE AND FROM THE PERSPECTIVE OF A MULTI-ETHNIC EMPIRE.

terms.def: The Qing Court of Colonial Affairs, administering Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet according to their own statutes and indigenous laws.

cards.q: What did legal pluralism look like in the Qing empire?
cards.a: Territories administered by the COURT OF COLONIAL AFFAIRS (Lifan yuan) were governed by the MONGOL STATUTES; in Xinjiang the Sino-Muslim Regional Statutes applied; criminal cases among Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Kazakhs were decided by their INDIGENOUS LAWS and civil disputes by local custom, the sources including Islamic law. Manchu bannermen had their own penal code.

cards.q: What did the Qing do to the concept of China?
cards.a: It RECONCEIVED IT AS A MULTI-ETHNIC ENTITY rather than a purely Chinese one: it incorporated Manchuria, Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet plus Taiwan into its territory, and thereby defined what has since been regarded as China in modern times.

21.title: Cruel and unusual punishments
21.text: From the Sui to the Qing, with the exception of the Yuan, every code listed TWO REGULAR FORMS OF THE DEATH PENALTY: STRANGULATION AND DECAPITATION. Both end in death, but STRANGULATION WAS REGARDED AS THE LIGHTER PUNISHMENT BECAUSE IT LEFT THE CONDEMNED PERSON'S BODY WHOLE, whereas decapitation separated the head — hence their different symbolic reach into the afterlife. The same logic explains the DESECRATION OF A CORPSE (LUSHI) and SLICING (LINGCHI). Most executions were carried out in public FOR THEIR EXEMPLARY EFFECT ON THE PUBLIC AND THEIR SHAMING EFFECT ON THE GUILTY, usually at markets or at the crossroads of main streets — and for that reason an order that someone (an imperial relative or a high official) SHOULD TAKE HIS OWN LIFE AT HOME was regarded as a MERCIFUL FAVOUR. LINGCHI, known in the West as 'death by a thousand cuts', was in fact the DISMEMBERMENT OF THE BODY AFTER THE PERSON HAD BEEN KILLED BY THE THIRD CUT. Xu quotes: 'AT LEAST AS PRACTISED IN THE LATE QING, LINGCHI WAS NOT A SLOW DEATH, NOR DID IT LEAVE THE VICTIM LINGERING ON THE THRESHOLD OF DEATH, NOR DID IT INVOLVE A THOUSAND CUTS. IT WAS A METHODICAL AND RELATIVELY RAPID TECHNIQUE OF PUTTING TO DEATH.' It originated in the state of Liao and in the Song as an AD HOC EXCEPTIONAL punishment, then became formalised, though some officials questioned its legitimacy along the way. The Qing code listed SEVENTEEN offences punishable by lingchi.

terms.def: Slicing: the dismemberment of the body after the person has been killed by the third cut. Not the slow death by a thousand cuts believed in the West.

cards.q: Why was strangulation a lighter punishment than decapitation?
cards.a: Because it LEFT THE CONDEMNED PERSON'S BODY WHOLE, whereas decapitation separated the head — the difference lay in the symbolic reach into the AFTERLIFE. The same logic stands behind the desecration of a corpse (lushi) and slicing (lingchi) as aggravated punishments.

cards.q: What was lingchi in fact?
cards.a: The dismemberment of the body AFTER THE PERSON HAD BEEN KILLED BY THE THIRD CUT. At least in the late Qing it was not a slow death, it did not leave the victim lingering on the threshold of death, and it did not involve a thousand cuts — it was a methodical and relatively rapid technique of putting to death. The Qing code listed seventeen offences punishable by it.

22.title: The Zhang case (1788): justice as balance
22.text: In 1788 a tenant farmer named ZHANG in Henan province, after a bitter quarrel with a neighbour, cut down THREE OF THE NEIGHBOUR'S SONS and left a fourth gravely wounded for dead. The governor sentenced him to death by lingchi and his wife and two small sons to banishment to the frontier as slaves. On review, however, Emperor QIANLONG held that ZHANG'S TWO SONS SHOULD BE CASTRATED. His reasoning: ZHANG HAD KILLED THREE OF HIS NEIGHBOUR'S SONS AND THE FOURTH, STILL FIGHTING FOR HIS LIFE, MIGHT ALSO DIE; SUCH ABOMINABLE ACTS OF CUTTING OFF SOMEONE'S FAMILY LINE CANNOT BE ADEQUATELY PUNISHED WITHOUT CUTTING OFF THE MURDERER'S FAMILY LINE AS WELL. He ordered that such a punishment for the children of such murderers should be a SUB-STATUTE to be followed in similar cases. Xu interprets it thus: QIANLONG'S REASONING SHOWS A SENSE OF JUSTICE THAT VALUED THE FAMILY LINE AND RESTED ON THE IDEA THAT A CRIME IS MET BY A FITTING PUNISHMENT SO AS TO RESTORE THE BALANCE OF YIN AND YANG. BUT THIS WAS NOT A UNIVERSAL VIEW: the criticism of lingchi by some officials ran precisely along the lines that THE STATE SHOULD NOT PUNISH AN OFFENDER BY COMMITTING THE SAME ACT ITSELF — that is, they opposed 'AN EYE FOR AN EYE' and 'MIRROR PUNISHMENTS'.

cards.q: How did Qianlong justify castrating the murderer's sons in the case of 1788?
cards.a: That Zhang had killed three of his neighbour's sons and the fourth might also die; SUCH AN ABOMINABLE CUTTING OFF OF A FAMILY LINE cannot be adequately punished without cutting off the murderer's family line as well. It shows a sense of justice that values the family line and rests on RESTORING THE BALANCE OF YIN AND YANG by a fitting punishment — and the emperor ordered it as a sub-statute for the future.

cards.q: Was 'mirror punishment' uncontested in China?
cards.a: No. The criticism of lingchi by some officials ran that THE STATE SHOULD NOT PUNISH AN OFFENDER BY COMMITTING THE SAME ACT ITSELF — they therefore opposed 'an eye for an eye' and mirror punishments.

23.title: Collective punishment, the cangue and tattooing
23.text: From the pre-imperial state of Qin under Shang Yang, one of the cruel punishments was TO EXECUTE THE ADULT MALE RELATIVES AND ENSLAVE THE ADULT FEMALE AND MINOR RELATIVES of an offender. This collective punishment rested on the idea of THE PARAMOUNT IMPORTANCE OF THE FAMILY LINE AND OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE CONDUCT OF AN INDIVIDUAL. In the early dynasties it concerned THREE BRANCHES (and up to five, seven, nine); how they were counted was later disputed, but it was generally held that the 'three branches' were the relatives of the offender's FATHER, MOTHER AND WIFE. In the imperial era collective punishment appeared ONLY OCCASIONALLY, typically when an emperor felt offended by a conspiracy or by his own paranoia about one, or by an official criticising his policy — THE MING WAS THE LAST DYNASTY IN WHICH IT OCCURRED. Until the Qing, however, the punishment of abominable crimes still included THE BANISHMENT OF FAMILY MEMBERS TO THE FRONTIER AS STATE SLAVES. Two supplementary punishments: WEARING THE CANGUE (a wooden board locking in the neck and hands) IN PUBLIC, at the gate of the county office, for a set period; and TATTOOING THE CHARACTERS FOR 'BANISHMENT' ON THE FACE or 'ROBBERY' OR 'THEFT' ON THE RIGHT FOREARM. They served two purposes: they provided MORE DEGREES OF PUNISHMENT so as to fit offences committed in varying circumstances, and they were a form of PUBLIC SHAMING with an exemplary effect the state took seriously. How seriously is shown by one provision: UNDER THE QING CODE, THE REMOVAL OF A TATTOO BY A FORMER CONVICT WITHOUT PERMISSION WAS A SEPARATE OFFENCE PUNISHED BY SIXTY STROKES AND RETATTOOING.

cards.q: What did collective punishment rest on and when did it last occur?
cards.a: On the idea of the PARAMOUNT IMPORTANCE OF THE FAMILY LINE and of COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY for an individual's conduct: execute the adult males and enslave the female and minor relatives, the 'three branches' being the relatives of the offender's father, mother and wife. In the imperial era it appeared only occasionally, typically from an emperor's offended paranoia — and the MING was the last dynasty in which it occurred.

cards.q: What purpose did the cangue and tattooing serve, and what does the punishment for removing a tattoo prove?
cards.a: They provided MORE DEGREES OF PUNISHMENT so as to fit the circumstances, and they were a form of PUBLIC SHAMING with an exemplary effect. How seriously the state took this is shown by the fact that under the Qing code the REMOVAL OF A TATTOO WITHOUT PERMISSION WAS A SEPARATE OFFENCE punished by sixty strokes and retattooing.

24.title: Three points that should stay with you
24.text: The author's own summary, and it is the single best answer to an exam question on Chinese criminal law. FIRST: the ideas of the MANDATE OF HEAVEN AND OF HEAVEN-HUMAN INTERACTION shaped the conception of the political-social-moral order in such a way that it RESTED ON THE IMPERIAL SYSTEM AND THE PATRIARCHAL FAMILY — and justice had THREE FUNCTIONS: TO PUNISH DEVIATIONS FROM THAT ORDER, TO FULFIL HEAVENLY REASON PROPERLY AND REGULATE HUMAN RELATIONS, AND TO RESTORE THE BALANCE OF YIN AND YANG. SECOND: over two millennia the Chinese penal codes grew towards ever greater sophistication and comprehensiveness; FROM THE TANG IN THE 7TH CENTURY AT THE LATEST, THE CODE COVERED ALL ASPECTS OF THE ORDER, INCLUDING ADMINISTRATIVE, CIVIL AND CRIMINAL MATTERS. THIRD: the regular punishments moved FROM BODILY MUTILATION TOWARDS MORE RATIONAL AND MORE HUMANE FORMS, even though some cruel and unusual punishments remained and beating as bodily pain continued to be used for lesser offences. Punishments could be redeemed by FINES for aged or disabled offenders or under an amnesty. And one sentence that is easy to overlook and is the most interesting of all for legal history: IMPRISONMENT WAS NOT UNDERSTOOD AS A PUNISHMENT.

cards.q: Sum up the development of Chinese law in three points.
cards.a: 1) The Mandate of Heaven and Heaven-human interaction shaped an order resting on the IMPERIAL SYSTEM AND THE PATRIARCHAL FAMILY, and justice was to punish deviations, fulfil heavenly reason and regulate human relations, and restore the balance of yin and yang. 2) The codes grew in sophistication — from the Tang at the latest they covered administrative, civil and criminal matters. 3) Punishments moved from bodily mutilation towards more humane forms, though cruel punishments remained.

cards.q: How was imprisonment regarded in imperial China?
cards.a: IMPRISONMENT WAS NOT UNDERSTOOD AS A PUNISHMENT. The five-part system of punishments was death, banishment, penal labour, whipping and beating — prison served for detention, not for punishment.
